Jot is a way to keep a journal as plain text. You can write it in any text editor, on a phone, on an e-ink writer like InkDeck, or in the Jot workspace in your browser. Nothing has to be filled in, and nothing is required except your words.

This guide covers everything you need to write a .jot file by hand. It takes about ten minutes to read, and you can stop after the first section.

Start with just writing

A .jot file can be nothing but sentences. This is a complete journal:

The rain made the room feel quieter. I wanted to remember that.

Everything else in this guide is optional. Add it when it helps, skip it when it doesn't.

Writing in the browser workspace

The Write workspace opens with a blank editor on desktop and mobile Chromium browsers. If you have written here before, your saved writing returns. The top bar keeps the filename, browser and device save status, Open, Save and Tools nearby.

Headings, emphasis, lists and links display as you type on the writing surface. Tools → Source editing exposes the complete plain-text journal; Live editing returns without converting or rewriting it. Structured blocks have Edit source buttons. Charts and queries retain their source cards here; Tools → Page preview renders them with the whole journal's context. The Tools menu also offers Write only and Side by side views for page layout and printing.

In secure desktop Chromium browsers, Open connects a selected device file and Save writes back on explicit request. Save as chooses another destination. Ctrl+S / Cmd+S saves; add Shift for Save as. Device access is separate from browser autosave. External file changes stop saving so you can keep both versions. Adding attachments to plain text chooses a new .jotz destination. Handles last only for this visit. When file access is unavailable, Save downloads a copy instead. Tools → Download journal always keeps a separate copy. Locked journals Save as an encrypted download; direct device writes are currently for unlocked .jot and .jotz documents. Other exports and printing are unencrypted.

Extra controls stay closed until you need them. In Tools, choose Journal tools for the journal button row, Formatting controls for formatting buttons and Colors, or Writing options for suggestions and writing hints. Attached files opens the attachment list; it also appears when the journal contains files.

  • Bold, Italic, Code and Link edit the selected source. Heading, Task, Bullets, Numbers and Quote format the selected lines. Indent and Outdent move those lines by two spaces. The text remains ordinary Jot/Markdown.
  • Ctrl+B / Cmd+B and Ctrl+I / Cmd+I format words. Tab and Shift+Tab indent lists or multiple selected lines; Tab in ordinary prose continues keyboard navigation.
  • Continue lists on Enter continues bullets, numbering, quotes and tasks. New tasks start unchecked. Enter on an empty item leaves the list; Shift+Enter inserts an ordinary newline. Turn the option off for manual line breaks. It is remembered locally.
  • Find & replace (Ctrl+F / Cmd+F while writing) searches literal text in this journal, with match-case and whole-word options. Next and Previous wrap around. Replace and Replace all are explicit; replacement text is literal, including $.
  • Outline jumps to a dated entry or heading. Headings inside code and comments stay out of the outline.
  • Tools (Ctrl+K / Cmd+K) searches writing tools and journal workflows. Type a command, then choose it or press Enter. Arrow keys move through results and Escape closes the menu. Searching alone does not edit the journal.
  • Entry templates, available in Tools, offers daily reflections, weekly and monthly recaps, meetings and freewriting. Choose a template, edit its blank prompts in the review field, then Insert. It inserts after your selection without replacing selected words. These are starting points for your own writing; no experiences, dates, locations or measurements are filled in.

Formatting, replacements and template insertion support the browser's Undo command (Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z). Your writing still autosaves in this browser, and Download keeps a separate .jot file (or .jotz with attachments). Current-time and location capture remain manual actions.

Dates organise your writing

A heading that starts with a date makes an entry for that day. Anything after the date, after a |, is up to you (a weekday, a place, a word):

### 2026-10-25 | Sunday

A slow morning. Tea, then a walk.

### 2026-10-26 | Monday

Back to work. It went better than I expected.
  • The date is always YEAR-MONTH-DAY, like 2026-10-25.
  • Any heading level works (#, ##, ### …); most people use ### for days and # for the month.
  • One file can hold one day, a month, or years. A file is not a day: the dates inside it are what count.
  • The same date can appear twice (a morning and an evening entry); both are kept.

Quick marks at the start of a line

Start a line with one of these and a space:

Write It means
[ ] Call the pharmacy a task to do
[x] Call the pharmacy done
[>] Call the pharmacy moved to another day
[<] Call the pharmacy scheduled for later
[-] Call the pharmacy not doing it after all (cancelled)
[!] Call the pharmacy important (an open task, marked high priority)
o 4:00p Dentist an event
? Why am I so tired on Mondays a question to come back to
! A shelf by the door for keys an idea 
### 2026-10-26 | Monday

[x] Water the plants
[ ] Return the library book
[>] Fix the bike light
o 6:30p Soup night with a neighbour
? What would make tomorrow easier
! A shelf by the door for keys

A mark needs words after it: [ ] on its own is just text until you write the task. That is how the templates work: an empty [ ] line is a box waiting for you.

A line that continues the item above starts with two spaces:

[ ] Plan the weekend
  Ask Sam about Saturday first.

Ordinary formatting (Markdown)

Jot uses Markdown for everything else, so what you may already know works:

#### Something worth keeping

**Bold**, *italic*, ~~crossed out~~.

- a list item
- another one

1. first
2. second

> A line someone said that I want to remember.

| Moment | Note |
| --- | --- |
| Morning | Quiet enough to think |

- [ ] task (with a dash) also shows as a checklist, but only plain [ ] task lines count as Jot tasks (with states like moved or cancelled), and they are quicker to type.

More ways to mark words

Jot adds a few marks that many Markdown editors (Obsidian, Typora, iA Writer) and GitHub also understand:

I want to remember ==this part== most.
Something ++underlined++, and E = mc^2^.
A claim that needs its source.[^where]

-> A line in the middle of the page <-

> [!TIP]
> Headphones helped more than pushing through.

[^where]: Overheard on the bus, 26 October.
You write You get
==words== a highlight, like a marker pen
++words++ underlined words
x^2^ superscript (no spaces inside)
[^name] and, on a line of its own, [^name]: the note a footnote: a small number in the text and the note at the end of the page. A note can go on over lines indented by two spaces
-> words <- a line centred on the page
> [!NOTE] on the first line of a quote (also TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION) a callout box, as on GitHub

Each mark needs a letter just inside it, so ordinary writing like a == b, C++ or 2 ^ 3 stays as you typed it. Inside `code` nothing is a mark.

Notes in the margin, and things only you see

  • [[ like this ]] on its own line is a margin note: a remark beside the writing, not part of it.
  • Lines between /* and */ (each on its own line) are hidden: they stay in the file but are not shown when the journal is read. Hidden is not secret: anyone who opens the file can read them.
[[ written on the bus, so it's short ]]

/*
Things to look up later: the name of that song.
*/

Numbers, ratings and other data (records)

When you want something a program can count (sleep hours, energy, a mood), put it in a record. A record starts with :::record and a type, has one name: value per line, and ends with ::::

:::record observation #sleep-2026-10-26
bed: 11:40p
wake: 7:10a
quality: 3
:::
  • The part after # is an id. It is optional, but it must be unique in the file if you use it.
  • Names are lowercase, with dashes instead of spaces (minutes-outside:).
  • An empty value (quality:) means "not filled in", which is fine.
  • For several lines, write name: | and indent the lines under it by two spaces.
:::record reflection
body: |
  Today was hard, and I still did the one thing.
  That counts.
:::

Scales. A rating means more when the scale is written down once. Templates do this for you at the top of the file:

:::record scale #scale-energy
name: energy
kind: ordinal
minimum: 1
maximum: 5
anchor-low: empty
anchor-high: full
:::

:::record measurement #energy-2026-10-26
metric: energy
scale: #scale-energy
value: 3
:::

To fill in a rating, type the number after value:. Leaving it empty is always allowed: an empty value never counts as a zero.

Units. A measurement can say what its number counts in: unit: h for hours, unit: km, unit: ml.

Charts of your numbers

Numbers you write day after day can be drawn as a chart, so a week's sleep or steps shows at a glance. Add a chart record:

### 2026-10-26 | Monday

:::record measurement #sleep-2026-10-26
metric: sleep
unit: h
value: 7.5
:::

:::record observation #today-2026-10-26
steps: 8200
:::

### 2026-10-27 | Tuesday

:::record measurement #sleep-2026-10-27
metric: sleep
unit: h
value: 6
:::

:::record chart #week-2026-10-26
metrics: sleep, steps
:::
  • What it charts: metrics: names the numbers, by their metric: (in a measurement) or their field name (steps: in any other record). Leave metrics: out to chart every number.
  • Which days: a chart inside a dated entry covers that entry's week, Monday to Sunday. start: and end: (dates) choose other days; a chart outside any entry covers the days that have numbers.
  • How: style: line (the default) or style: bars.
  • Each number gets its own small chart, on its own scale, with the days along the bottom, the week's average as a dashed line and a summary (avg 6.8 h · 6–7.5 h · 2/7 days). A measurement with a scale: is charted from the scale's minimum to its maximum. Days with nothing written are gaps, never zeros. Two numbers for one metric on one day are averaged.
  • Where you see it: the workspace (Write), the template editor's Page view and the Jot extension for VS Code draw it. Anywhere else the record shows as the few lines above, which still say what it charts.

Links between days and records

Every dated heading is a place you can link to: write the date after #. A record with an ID (:::record note #plan) can be linked by its ID the same way. Links work anywhere you write: in paragraphs, lists, tables, quotes, footnotes, tasks and margin notes.

### 2026-10-25 | Sunday

Started sketching the garden plan.

### 2026-10-26 | Monday

Back to what I began [yesterday](#2026-10-25), and to [the plan](#plan).

:::record note #plan
body: Beans along the fence.
relation: continues #2026-10-25
:::
  • In the preview, a link jumps to that day or record, and each one shows a short Linked from line: the days and records that point at it.
  • A link to something that isn't there (a typo, or a date with no heading yet) still shows as written, and the checker lists it as an unresolved link. Nothing stops you writing.
  • If two headings share a date, a link goes to the first.
  • Records link too: relation: continues #2026-10-25, member: #plan and source: #2026-10-25 point at a day or record when the value is just the # link (after the kind, for relation).
  • Another file: [last month](september.jot#2026-09-30) is kept as written. Jot never opens or fetches the other file to check it.

Lists that find things for you (queries)

A query record asks a question of the journal it is in: which tasks are still open, what you tagged #health this week, how much you slept on average this month. The answer is worked out each time the page is shown, so it is never out of date, and the file only holds the question:

### 2026-10-26 | Monday

[ ] Call the dentist @phone #health
[x] Walk round the park #health
[!] Post the letter

:::record measurement #sleep-2026-10-26
metric: sleep
unit: h
value: 7.5
:::

:::record query #open-health
label: Still to do for my health
show: tasks
status: open
tag: health
:::

:::record query #sleep-this-week
label: Sleep this week
show: numbers
metric: sleep
period: week
stat: average
:::

The page shows each query as one plain sentence ("1 open task tagged #health.") and a table of what it found.

  • What to show: show: tasks, events, entries (dated sections) or numbers. This is the one field a query needs.
  • Which ones: status: (open, completed, migrated, scheduled, cancelled; several with commas mean any of them), priority: high, tag: and context: (several with commas mean all of them), text: (words it contains) and, for numbers, metric:.
  • Which days: period: day, week or month counts from the entry the query is written in (a week is Monday to Sunday), or from its own date:; start: and end: choose dates instead. With neither, every date counts, and so do tasks written before the first date.
  • How many: stat: count is the default; numbers can also have sum, average, min or max, each metric on its own. limit: 20 shows only the first 20 rows (the sentence still counts them all; 50 is the default).
  • Mistakes are shown, not hidden. A word the query doesn't know (status: opne, a blank tag:, a metric the journal doesn't have) shows what is wrong where the answer would be, and in the workspace's checks, instead of quietly showing nothing or everything.
  • A query never changes your writing and never runs anything. On the command line, jot query journal.jot prints the answers, and jot query journal.jot --show tasks --status open --tag health asks one without writing it down.

Palettes and moodboards

For designers and artists: a palette record keeps colors as text, one color: line each, a hex code then a name.

:::record palette #autumn-zine
label: Autumn zine
color: #c0392b brick red
color: #f4d03f mustard
color: #234 deep slate
:::
  • The page draws swatches that always print the name and hex code in words, in black or white, whichever reads better on that color. Color is never the only clue. Three digits (#234) are short for six (#223344); transparency is not part of a swatch.
  • A color Jot can't read (color: brick) stays exactly as you wrote it, and the page shows a note in its place, with a warning under Checks.
  • Copy palette CSS and Copy palette JSON in Tools copy the palette your cursor is in (or the nearest one before it) as CSS custom properties (:root { --brick-red: #c0392b; }) or as JSON. Add to palette ＋, beside the color menu, writes the chosen color into that palette, or starts one.

A moodboard record gathers pictures you've attached, each image: a path then a few words saying what it shows. caption: and credit: lines after a picture belong to it; color: lines add swatches.

:::record moodboard #rain-study
label: Rain study
image: assets/boots.jpg Wet boots on the bus floor
caption: Tuesday, 8am
credit: my phone
image: assets/ticket.png A crumpled blue bus ticket
color: #1f3a8a ink blue
body: Grey, wet, a little blue.
:::

The page lays the pictures out in a grid that fits the screen. A picture that isn't attached shows its path and description instead; nothing is fetched from the internet. Two or more pictures on their own in one paragraph are laid out the same way.

A few other things

  • Page break: === on its own line, after an empty line, starts a new page when the journal is printed.
  • Time labels: a line like .0830 - KITCHEN (a dot, then a label) marks a scene or a moment in the day.
  • Tags and places: #walk (a tag) and @home (a context, where or with whom) can go anywhere in a sentence. (The specification defines them; the tools here keep them as ordinary words for now and don't yet list or search them.)
  • Metadata: a block at the very top between two --- lines describes the whole file. Templates add one; you never need to:
---
Jot: 1.0
Title: October notebook
---

### 2026-10-01 | Thursday

A new notebook.
  • When a mark should just be text, put a backslash before it: \[ ] this is not a task or \# not a heading.

Beautiful pages: styles, printing and sharing

Write quickly; the workspace (Write) turns your jottings into formatted pages as you type. Dated headings read as dates ("Monday, 26 October 2026"), tasks show whether they are done, moved, scheduled or cancelled, events, questions and ideas get their signs, #tags and @places are marked, [[margin notes]] sit beside the text and .0830 - KITCHEN reads "08:30 · KITCHEN".

Open Preview. Set Look to Typed, then Style chooses the look:

Style What it looks like
Journal a book page: a classic serif, dates in small capitals, a drop cap opening each day, margin notes in the margin
Notes clean and modern: a sans serif, each date as a bar, tags as coloured chips, checkboxes, tidy tables
Plain simple and quiet

To keep or share the pages:

  • Print / PDF prints them on the Paper you choose (A5, A4, Letter, pocket or your own), with book margins and page numbers (Journal and Notes). Choose "Save as PDF" in the print dialog for a PDF.
  • Download page ↓ saves one .html file with the formatted pages inside it, charts as pictures and attached pictures included. It opens in any browser, on any device, without the internet, and prints as nicely as the workspace does. Send it to someone, or keep it beside the .jot.

The .jot file never changes: the style is only how it is shown. In VS Code, the jot.preview.style setting chooses the same styles, and Jot: Export as HTML saves the same page.

Handwritten pages on a dot grid

The workspace (Write) can show your journal as if you had written it by hand in a dot-grid notebook, and print it that way:

  1. Open Preview, then set Look to Handwritten.
  2. Choose a Hand: Pen (a natural pen hand; each letter comes in three shapes, so two es side by side are never quite the same), Neat print or Marker. Choose an Ink colour, and how far apart the dots are (Dots every 4 to 7 mm; 5 mm is the usual notebook).
  3. Pick the Paper (A5, A4, Letter, pocket or your own size), then Print / PDF. In the print dialog keep the margins at Default and the scale at 100%.

Every line of writing sits on a row of dots, page after page: the printed dots and the letters come out together, so the page looks filled in by hand. Headings take two rows, a blank row separates paragraphs, and charts, tables and pictures are rounded up to whole rows so nothing after them slips off the grid. Dashed lines in the preview show where each printed page ends.

Task boxes are drawn in pencil, and not all the same way: a square closed with an overlap, one left open at a corner, one gone over twice, a softer rounded one. A done task gets a tick that runs past the box the way a quick pen does: a plain check, one with a little hook, a long flick, or two quick strokes. No two boxes in a row are drawn alike. Each word leans and sits a little differently, and the wobbles are worked out from the words themselves, so the same journal always prints the same. Rewrite ↻ writes it again with other wobbles and letter shapes; your words never change. Turn Dots off to print the handwriting on plain paper, or on paper that already has a dot grid.

The template editor's Page view and the VS Code extension can show the handwritten look too, and Download page ↓ keeps a handwritten page with its hand inside the file.

Plain and packaged files

  • .jot is plain text: what you see is what is in it. This is what you write and what templates make.
  • .jotz is a packaged journal: one file that carries pictures, scans or handwriting together with the writing (it is a ZIP inside).

The Jot workspace opens both and saves whichever fits: plain .jot when there are no attachments, .jotz when there are. A text editor or InkDeck works with .jot; to get the writing out of a .jotz, open it in the workspace (or unzip it and open journal.txt).

  • .jotlock is a locked journal: a .jot or .jotz encrypted with a passphrase. Only its ways in open it: the passphrase, a recovery code or a passkey you added (below).

Locking a journal

In the workspace, Lock with a passphrase encrypts the journal with the browser's own built-in cryptography (AES-256-GCM). Nothing is sent anywhere. Unless you untick it, you also get a recovery code: a second way in for when the passphrase is forgotten, shown once. Save it in a password manager or write it down, away from the journal. From then on:

  • this browser keeps only an encrypted copy of the writing and its attachments;
  • Download locked saves a .jotlock, which opens in the workspace (Open a journal) or with the command line (jot unlock);
  • reloading the page asks for the passphrase before showing anything. Remove it from this browser deletes the locked copy here if you no longer need it;
  • Ways in lists what opens the journal, and lets you add a passkey or security key, make a new recovery code, change the passphrase, remove one, or Remove the lock to go back to an ordinary journal. Each change asks for a way in you already have. A passphrase or recovery code always stays.
  • Passkeys and security keys: a passkey on your phone or computer, or a key such as a YubiKey, unlocks with a touch, a fingerprint, your face or a PIN. It works only on this site, and only where the browser and the key support it (if not, you are told). A synced passkey is as safe as the account it syncs with, and someone can make you unlock with your face or finger more easily than make you tell a passphrase: if that worries you, keep to the passphrase.
  • Lock again, in Preferences, clears the journal from the page after 5, 15 (the standard) or 60 minutes with no typing or clicking, saving it (locked) first, so a journal left open on a shared computer doesn't stay open. Never keeps it open until you close the page.
  • Your password manager can save the passphrase: Jot names it after the journal, so separate journals get separate entries.

Things to know first:

  • Nobody can reset it. Jot never keeps or sends your passphrase, recovery code or passkey. Without one of them, nobody can open the journal, you included.
  • Copies you downloaded keep the ways in they had then: removing a passphrase or passkey does not reach them.
  • Other exports are not encrypted: Markdown, calendar and CSV files, a downloaded page and printing. Copies you downloaded before locking are not locked either.
  • A locked file's name, size and dates still show, and a lock does not help if someone uses your browser while the journal is unlocked.

Where to write

  • Any text editor, on a computer or a phone. Save the file with a .jot ending. (For colours, see Colours in your text editor.)
  • InkDeck, the e-ink writing firmware for the Xteink X3/X4: it creates .jot files for you.
  • The Jot workspace (Write, on this site): a plain editor with optional preview, charts, method ideas and attachments.
  • VS Code, with the Jot extension: colours for Jot's marks and a live page preview with charts. See Colours in your text editor.
  • The template editor: design the structure once and get a ready-made file for the month, a dated entry a day, to fill in. See Using the template editor.

Making the workspace comfortable

Everyone writes differently, so the workspace (Write) lets you change how it looks, one thing at a time. None of these choices go into your journal: they are remembered in this browser only, and the page works the same without them.

  • Writing preferences (in Tools): text size, line spacing, line length and how dense the controls are; higher contrast; reduced motion (your system's reduce-motion setting is always followed too); and, separately, whether to show the page preview, the parser and writing-check tabs, the word and check counts, and decoration like small headings and taglines. Back to standard settings undoes them. Printing and Download page are not affected.
  • Focus mode shows only the writing, its name and whether it is saved. Press Escape or Leave focus mode to see everything again.
  • Quick note ＋ adds one line to the end of today's dated entry (making the entry if there is none) and leaves your cursor where it was, unless you tick the box to go there. Undo (Ctrl+Z) takes it back.
  • Coming back: your cursor and scroll position return when you reopen the page. If you like, write a short note for next time in Preferences, such as "Next: the paragraph about the walk". It is shown when you come back, with Back to where I was, Start at the end and Dismiss. Nothing counts days, keeps streaks or asks you to catch up.
  • Your day: if your day doesn't end at midnight (a night shift, a late bedtime), set My day starts at in Preferences. Before that hour it is still yesterday for Today ＋, Quick note ＋, Carry tasks forward and Week review, so a night stays in one entry. Back to standard settings keeps it, like your note.

Colours in your text editor

VS Code has a Jot extension (in the vscode/ folder of the Jot project): dates, tasks, events, records and their numbers in colour, and Jot: Open Preview to the Side (Ctrl+K V, Cmd+K V on a Mac) for a live page preview that draws your charts. Jot: Insert a Week Chart writes a chart record for this week. Until it is in the Marketplace, install it from the folder: run npx @vscode/vsce package there, then Extensions → … → Install from VSIX.

Other editors don't know .jot yet, but Jot is Markdown underneath. Tell your editor to treat .jot as Markdown and you get headings, lists, bold and tables in colour. (Jot's own marks, like o events and records, show as plain text.)

Editor How
VS Code (and VSCodium, Cursor), without the extension Open a .jot file, click the language name at the bottom right ("Plain Text"), choose Configure File Association for '.jot'…, then Markdown
Sublime Text Open a .jot file, then View → Syntax → Open all with current extension as… → Markdown
JetBrains (IntelliJ, PyCharm …) Settings → Editor → File Types → Markdown, add *.jot
Neovim Add vim.filetype.add({ extension = { jot = 'markdown' } }) to your config
Vim Add autocmd BufRead,BufNewFile *.jot setfiletype markdown to your .vimrc
Emacs (with markdown-mode) Add (add-to-list 'auto-mode-alist '("\\.jot\\'" . markdown-mode)) to your init file

On a phone, any app that edits plain text files works; colour is a bonus, not a need.

Real diaries to look at

The Examples page has whole diaries as Jot: Samuel Pepys's nine and a half years, The Diary of a Nobody and Wilfrid Scawen Blunt's diaries, a dated entry for each day. Open one in the workspace to see how a long journal reads, or download it.

Small habits that help

  • One file a month is easy to find and small enough to type into anywhere. Name it by the month: 2026-10.jot.
  • Write the date heading first, then anything: a word is enough.
  • Skipped days need nothing. There is no catching up.
  • Write down how you use it: Write your own manual takes ten minutes and makes the system yours.
  • Keep a copy somewhere else. A .jot file is just a file: back it up like a photo.

The full rules are in the Jot specification. You won't need them to write.

Color in handwritten pages

New previews use Handwritten; an existing Look preference is kept. The same colors appear in handwritten preview, Print / PDF, and Download page (standalone HTML).

Choose Tools → Formatting controls, then Colors. Select words on one line, choose a palette color or a custom color, choose Text ink, Highlight, Strikethrough or Underline, then press Apply color. Keep the selection and apply another effect to combine them. To change an effect again, select the same formatted words and apply the new color; the new color replaces that effect in the selected spans. Clear colors removes color spans fully included in the selection; select their brackets and attributes too. Ordinary bold, italic, links and writing remain intact. Undo works in the writing field.

Colors are part of the saved journal, rather than browser-only preferences:

[Rose-colored writing]{ink=#b33951}
[A yellow highlight]{highlight=#ffe680}
[Changed my mind]{strike=#c0392b}
[Keep this thought]{underline=#245ac2}
[All together]{ink=#1f3a8a highlight=#ffe680 strike=#c0392b underline=#245ac2}

You can nest spans and use bold or italic inside them. Each color uses six hexadecimal digits; custom CSS is not supported. A color span stays on one source line. Handwriting keeps the chosen hand and grid spacing. Contrast feedback compares ink to light paper, or a highlight to the default blue ink; check the actual preview when combining colors. Choose color printing and enable background graphics if your browser requires it. Physical print and mobile print results still need device checks.

Highlights with a human hand

For Highlight, the Stroke control offers Marker (a broad translucent pass), Brush (overlapping soft passes), and Pencil (several loose strokes). Repeated highlights have different edges and coverage, including ordinary ==highlight== marks. Rewrite ↻ makes another variation of the handwriting and highlights; it keeps your words and chosen colors. The variation stays consistent on reload, print, and HTML export until you rewrite it again.

[A broad marker]{highlight=#ffe680 highlight-style=marker}
[A softer brush]{highlight=#ffc7df highlight-style=brush}
[Loose pencil strokes]{highlight=#91bcf0 highlight-style=pencil}

Reference color palettes

The color menu and Show color swatches offer 71 colors from the supplied Mildliner, soft-color and pastel references. They are grouped by collection and labeled with their hex values. Lemon yellow (#fddd13) is the default highlight, including ==ordinary highlights==. The palette is available for text ink, highlights, strikethrough and underline; custom colors remain available. Soft colors are often best behind darker ink—check the contrast message when using them as text. Highlight strokes are translucent, so their appearance on paper is softer than the solid color swatch. Existing journal colors are preserved.

How highlighter and ink combine

Highlighter strokes sit on top of the writing and blend with the ink underneath, like a translucent marker on paper. Changing the text ink changes the visible result under the same highlight. The source keeps both colors separately; the effect carries through to Typed and Handwritten preview, print, PDF and standalone HTML. Marker, brush and pencil use the same blending rule.

Albums, playlists and Spotify short links

An entry can hold any number of music references:

#### Music for this week

- Album: [An album to return to](spotify:album:4aawyAB9vmqN3uQ7FjRGTy)
- Playlist: [My writing mix](spotify:playlist:37i9dQZF1DXcBWIGoYBM5M)
- spotify: track:11dFghVXANMlKmJXsNCbNl

Copy a Spotify URI, or keep the type and ID from a share URL: https://open.spotify.com/album/ID becomes spotify:album:ID. The types are track, album, playlist, artist, episode and show. A space after spotify: is optional. Named Markdown links show your label; bare short references show “Spotify album”, “Spotify playlist”, and so on. Each becomes an ordinary link in the page preview and HTML export. Reading an entry does not contact Spotify or load music automatically. Paste the same short reference into Music player ♫ to load it for listening while you write. These are links to collections; the music itself is not copied into your journal or its .jotz package. You can always use a normal HTTPS link for other services.

IMDb and YouTube background media

An entry can collect films, TV, episodes, videos and playlists alongside music:

#### Background media

- [Background film](imdb:tt0133093)
- [TV series](imdb:tt0386676)
- [Video](youtube:dQw4w9WgXcQ)
- [Video playlist](youtube:playlist:PL1234567890abcdef)

Use an actual provider ID from the link you want to save. IMDb uses imdb:tt… for title IDs (films, series and individual episodes). YouTube uses youtube:VIDEO_ID, optionally youtube:video:VIDEO_ID, or youtube:playlist:PLAYLIST_ID. A space after the first colon is optional. Bare shortcodes show a provider/type label; Markdown links give them a name. IMDb identifies the title and does not provide playback. These references do not fetch titles, ratings or thumbnails or embed videos automatically. The shared preview and HTML export expand them into ordinary HTTPS links.

In Music & background media, paste one reference per line, optionally Name | reference, and add the mixed list to the entry. Full IMDb title URLs and simple YouTube video/playlist URLs are shortened on insertion. Video links with timestamps or both a video and a playlist remain full URLs so their context is preserved. Existing journal writing is never automatically rewritten. The persistent writing player remains Spotify-only; YouTube references open YouTube when you follow them.

Find music IDs while typing

Open Music & background media → Find a song or album ID and enable Search MusicBrainz as I type. Choose song recording, album (release group), album edition, composition or artist, then type at least three characters in the dedicated search box. After a short pause, suggestions show names, artists and available dates, versions or durations. Choose a result with the mouse or Tab and Enter. It goes into the reference review list; Add to this entry is still needed to change the journal.

Only the search box text and chosen entity type are sent to MusicBrainz, with no account cookies or journal content. Search is off by default and turns off when the dialog closes. Requests are debounced/rate-limited, old searches are cancelled, and recent results are cached only for this page session. Busy/offline services show an error and leave manual entry available. Result names are not verified matches: check the recording/version or album edition before selecting one.

Database links use musicbrainz:recording:UUID, musicbrainz:release-group:UUID, musicbrainz:release:UUID, musicbrainz:work:UUID or musicbrainz:artist:UUID. They identify the music independently of Spotify or YouTube. Existing service links remain useful for playback; the lookup does not guess a corresponding playback URL. IMDb and YouTube remain manual links or shortcodes; their online search is not part of this MusicBrainz lookup.

Local writing suggestions

The workspace can reuse names already in the open journal. It does not search other journals or contact a service.

  • Type # or @ followed by part of a tag/context to find existing names.
  • Start a Markdown link such as [See](#river to find an existing entry or record by its date, ID or label. Choose a result to finish the link. With an empty label ([](#river), the result supplies the entry/record name. Ambiguous duplicate targets are not offered. Ordinary headings without dates or record IDs do not become link targets.
  • Inside a measurement record, type metric:, unit: or scale: and part of a value. Metrics come from existing measurement records; units come from records for the same metric, and scales come from existing scale records. Different units stay separate choices. Selecting a metric does not fill or overwrite units, scales or values.

Suggestions appear after a short pause. Down/Up chooses a suggestion; Enter or Tab inserts the chosen one. Enter without choosing still adds a newline. Escape dismisses suggestions, and Control/Command+Space shows them again. Pointer selection works too. Insertion is undoable and replaces only the current tag, link or field value. Suggestions stay off while composing IME text or writing in code, metadata or hidden comments. Unrecognised writing is left as it is.

Choose Tools → Writing options, then uncheck Local suggestions to turn them off. Only that preference is remembered; the suggestion index stays in page memory and is rebuilt from the current journal. Opening another journal does not reuse the previous document's names.

People, places and reference books

People & Places opens a local reference-book manager. Create a book such as people.jot or places.jot, or open existing plain-text .jot files. Books stay separate from the current journal. Add a person or place, save the record to the book, then Download book to keep a file. “Remember these books in this browser” is optional; when off, loaded books last only for this page. Browser copies are not a substitute for downloaded files. Unloading removes a book from suggestions, not from your disk.

People can store display and alternative names, given/family names, pronouns, organization, several emails/phones/websites, a postal address, a reference to a place, and notes. Places can store alternative names, kind, two address lines, city/locality, region, postal code, country and two-letter country code, WGS84 latitude/longitude in decimal degrees, optional elevation and coordinate accuracy in metres, IANA timezone, phone/websites, directions, accessibility notes and general notes. No address, coordinates or timezone are detected, inferred, geocoded or fetched. Coordinates must be supplied as a valid pair; timezone is checked against the browser's IANA support. Accuracy is supplied by you, not inferred from the number of decimal places.

Example reference-book content (fictional):

:::record person #person-robin
label: Robin
alias: Bird
notes: A friend from the writing group.
:::

:::record place #place-river
label: Riverside café
address-line1: Example Street
locality: London
country-code: GB
latitude: 51.5
longitude: -0.12
timezone: Europe/London
accessibility: Step-free entrance
:::

With the relevant book open, start [Meet](#Robin or [](#Riverside in the journal and choose a suggestion. The result is a normal link such as [Robin](people.jot#person-robin) or [Riverside café](places.jot#place-river). Alternative names and a place's city/region/country can help find it. Existing explicit destinations, for example [](places.jot#River, restrict the search to that book. IDs remain stable when you rename someone or a place, and the book filename is part of the reference.

Clicking such a link in the workspace opens the record in People & Places. A missing book prompts you to open it; no file or website is fetched. Reference-book contents are not copied into journal downloads, .jotz files or HTML exports. Keep/share referenced files separately when needed; exported HTML retains a relative link, without the book's private details or interactive manager. Outside the workspace, cross-file navigation depends on the reader. Sharing a reference book shares its data: it is plain text, not encrypted. An OpenStreetMap link appears for valid coordinates, but contacts the map provider only if clicked.

A place's timezone describes that place. It does not change entry times or override the document's Timezone metadata. Person/place numeric fields, such as coordinates or postal codes, are not treated as measurement/chart data.

Entry timezone overrides

Declare a document default in the optional top metadata, then override a particular dated entry with @timezone::

---
Jot: 1.0
Timezone: America/Los_Angeles
---

### 2026-10-28 | In London
@timezone: Europe/London

o Call at 09:00

### 2026-10-29 | Back to the default

o Another call at 09:00

The override applies to the whole entry, ending at the next dated heading, even if that heading has the same date. It does not carry forward, rewrite a date/time, or use a linked place's timezone. Put the directive below the entry heading. Invalid or blank zones are warnings and leave that entry unresolved, rather than falling back to the device or document. Duplicate directives warn; the last applies. A directive in the undated preamble warns; use metadata for a document default. Code and comments stay literal.

In Write, place the cursor in an entry and choose Entry timezone. Choose an IANA timezone or UTC, or Use document default to remove the override. The page and HTML export show the effective zone beside the dated heading. Edits can be undone.

Calendar export resolves local timed events using their entry/document zone and writes unambiguous UTC instants. Explicit RFC 3339 event timestamps with offsets retain their own instant. Missing timezone information stays floating; an invalid declared zone, a nonexistent spring-forward time or a repeated fall-back time stops timed export with an explanation. For an ambiguous hour, use an event record with a complete offset-bearing timestamp, such as start: 2026-11-01T01:30:00-05:00. All-day dates and ordinary date-based queries keep their written calendar dates.

Current time and location in Chromium

Insert current time inserts the actual current date/time as a complete timestamp with an explicit offset. It uses the entry zone when declared, otherwise the document zone. If neither is declared, this explicit capture action uses the browser's zone and records the offset in the inserted timestamp; it does not resolve or reinterpret older writing. An invalid declared zone must be fixed first. The timestamp always uses the actual current date, even when the entry is backdated. One Undo removes it. No timestamps are automatically inserted while typing or on save.

Capture location opens a review dialog. Get current location makes one Chromium geolocation request, which requires HTTPS or localhost and may show the browser's permission prompt. The browser's location service may use network providers according to its settings. “Prefer a more precise position” is optional; the result's supplied accuracy is shown rather than promising GPS precision. There is no background watching or geocoding, and no address or physical timezone is inferred from the browser's device timezone.

After reviewing latitude, longitude, available accuracy/elevation and the capture instant, choose Insert location in entry (to insert a plain place record, including its coordinates), or Save as a place… (to review/name it in a separate reference book). Nothing is added on permission grant alone. Denial, unavailable positions, timeouts and results arriving after the dialog closes leave the journal unchanged. The one-time browser request itself has no cancellation API; closing discards its result. Location inserted in the journal travels with that file when shared. Buttons are keyboard accessible and tested in Chromium.

Daily entries and longer recaps

Jot prescribes no word count or duration for an entry, although applications and packages have file-size limits. A dated heading starts an entry; it can describe a day, an ongoing topic or a longer recap. Daily entries and weekly/monthly recaps can coexist. The recap's heading date identifies the entry, while a period record explicitly describes what it covers:

### 2026-11-01 | Sunday

Today's writing.

### 2026-11-01 | Weekly recap

:::record period #week-2026-10-26
label: Week of 26 October
start: 2026-10-26
end: 2026-11-02
:::

What mattered this week?

Period ends are exclusive, so this covers 26 October through 1 November. A monthly recap can use start: 2026-10-01 and end: 2026-11-01. A plain “Weekly recap” heading without a date stays inside the preceding dated entry. These are ordinary entries with explicit coverage, not new typed week/month navigation modes. A recap timezone describes that recap only; it never changes the original entries it references. Link to its period record ID when repeated dates would make a date-only link ambiguous.
